In short: the chicken and the egg all over again.
139) Contrary to a widespread belief, Kant did not completely deny the possibility of knowing reality independently of consciousness.

He maintained only that we can apply these categories to the spatiotemporal manifold.

Consequently, all knowledge that falls under the “categories” and the “principles” presented in the first part of the Transcendental Logic of the Critique of Pure Reason concerns not “things in themselves” but only the “appearances” of those things as they appear to human beings.
But this is not the place for a detailed discussion of Kant’s doctrine.

In recent years, however, it has begun to decline, even in Europe.

142) What is at issue here is the theory of knowledge—gnoseology—meaning the study of knowledge in the true sense, or, put differently, of convincing discourse.
Our claim is that this kind of study is impossible if knowledge is separated from reality.

It is possible, however, to study discourse while setting aside its power to convince. So-called “formal” logic, for example, studies discourse from the standpoint of its consistency, and therefore asks whether it is meaningful and coherent.
Grammar, in turn, sets consistency aside and studies the articulated structure of discourse.

Etymology studies the independently functioning elements that make up discourse—its “links,” or words. Syntax studies meaningful combinations of words without asking whether they contain a “logical” contradiction.
Syntax therefore accepts the grammatical correctness of a sentence such as “the black rectangular circle is white,” while rejecting a collection of words such as “he to the house do from always.”
So it can appear that logic and grammar study discourse independently of its relation to reality—independently of its “content,” that is, without asking whether the discourse is knowledge or not.
In reality, however, this is an illusion. But we cannot discuss that question here.
143) For ease of presentation, the discussion there will also be divided into different parts.
But those parts are inseparable in the sense that each presupposes the others.
The Phenomenology offered to the reader, by contrast, studies only one aspect of knowledge.
144) In his Phenomenology, Hegel studies both aspects at the same time.

His extraordinary stylistic ability enabled him to write the book in such a way that almost every sentence simultaneously describes—depending on how it is interpreted—both a stage in the development of knowledge as it reveals reality and an element of the reality revealed at that stage of knowledge.
Moreover, this aspect of reality is described simultaneously on both the ontological and the cosmological level. The meaning of these terms will be explained later.
Hegel’s Phenomenology therefore does more than prepare the possibility of knowledge. It also supplies the material needed to realize that knowledge in systematic philosophy.
But this method of presentation makes the book practically unreadable—or at the very least extremely difficult to understand.
I have therefore separated the two aspects.

And because a clear and broadly accessible presentation of the second aspect would have at least doubled the length of this already substantial book, I decided not to present the side concerning reality here.
Admittedly, in the systematic part I will therefore have to reconstruct the real aspect corresponding to each stage.
Still, it seems to me that this procedure will make both the Phenomenology itself and the logic of the Cosmology easier to understand.
Unfortunately, I have not managed to eliminate the real aspect completely. In other words, my Phenomenology is not perfectly uniform.

146) In this respect, Phenomenology is much closer to Plato’s theory of knowledge, as we find it in the Dialogues, than to the theory of knowledge presented in Kant’s Critiques—to say nothing of the neo-Kantians.
Plato too studies not abstract knowledge and opinion, but living human beings who actually hold that knowledge and those opinions.
He likewise does not separate form from content. He does not show us “cognition in general,” but the actual knowledge of the world and of humanity achieved by a concrete human being.
Plato’s theory of knowledge, however, is not historical.
The opinions he examines exist alongside one another, but they do not emerge from one another.
His theory of knowledge is therefore not “systematic”: it gives no guarantee that it is exhaustive, and it does not show why the opinions it studies necessarily arise, change, and disappear.

Race itself, by contrast, concerns the human being taken in actual reality.
The question of “races” therefore belongs to systematic philosophy—to Cosmology—whereas the question of “racist” theories belongs to Phenomenology.

Phenomenology knows, of course, that a human being without a body is nothing, and that human existence really presupposes animal or “biological” life and cannot be separated from it.

But the entire animal basis of human existence remains outside Phenomenology. Phenomenology presupposes it but does not discuss it.
The same must be said of discourse.
Phenomenology shows that discourse is not a primary phenomenon. It presupposes the specifically human, “negative” desire, which is itself based on animal desire.

As long as a tiger is a tiger, it always has the same essential qualities. Change those qualities and it ceases to be—and to be called—a tiger. A human being, by contrast, remains human despite undergoing essential changes. Sometimes the “background” included in a scientific explanation can even be the world as a whole. Theories of this kind, which seem to include “everything,” are often called “philosophical.” This reflects the correct but vague intuition that philosophical knowledge is omniscience, and vice versa.

But even here only one aspect of the natural world is being considered. The world described by such a theory contains no pine trees, mountains, or animals. And in any case it excludes human beings and the human world—above all, the physicist himself together with his theory.
That is precisely the problem, as we will now see.

An eye sees precisely the colour dark blue. It does not see the frequency of the vibrations.

Indeed, in the part of the natural world where these electromagnetic vibrations exist, there need not be any eye or cornflower at all. There may be only atoms and electrons—the same kinds of atoms and electrons that make up both the cornflower and the eye.
So even if these atoms can in some sense respond to electromagnetic waves, they certainly cannot see them.
159) Ontologically, we obviously cannot go any further, because beyond the limits of being there is nothing. We therefore cannot speak of the “cause” of being.

Theologians, admittedly, claim that beyond being there is God, who then becomes its cause or creator. But one of the fundamental tasks of philosophy, and of Ontology in particular, is precisely to prove that the concept of “God” is impossible.
Ontology therefore shows itself to be the “last” science—or, if one prefers, the “first”: prima philosophia.
160) To make this clearer, I will say only the following.
The first and fundamental question of Ontology is:
As for existence or actuality, it can be ideal or real, and real existence can in turn be natural or human.

The question is therefore whether there are distinct kinds of being corresponding to these kinds of existence, kinds that cannot be reduced to one another; or whether there is only one and the same being, which sometimes exists really, sometimes ideally, and so on.
This is the question of ontological “monism” versus ontological “pluralism,” including “dualism.”

“Spiritualism,” vulgar “materialism,” and “idealism” all maintain that being is one, but they define it very differently. Spiritualism defines it as “spiritual,” materialism as “material,” and idealism as “ideal”—as “consciousness in general.”

Pluralism can also take different forms. There can be a dualism that distinguishes human being from natural being while assigning ideal being to one or the other. Or there can be a dualism between real being and ideal being, with both human and natural being included under real being.
In every case, pluralism recognizes two or more kinds of being that cannot be reduced to one another.
From this we can see that the dispute between spiritualism and materialism, or between idealism and realism, is purely ontological.

There is hardly any disagreement that the phenomenon “human being” differs from the phenomenon “stone” or from the phenomenon “geometrical parabola.” Nor is there any real disagreement that the world divides into a human world and a natural world. Disagreement does arise over an “ideal” world, which can either be assigned to the human world or, as Plato does, separated off into an independent world of its own.
The real question is this: how can one and the same being exist in the form of these two worlds? That, for example, is the position of “materialism.”
